threads.thread_goal: Align on scope and target operating model for centralised management.

messages.text:
Kicking off the Launch of Centralised Residential Property Management Model project. Objective is to move to a centralised way of running our existing residential portfolio, improving occupancy, compliance and tenant satisfaction while staying within current regulations and without major capex.

For scope: my proposal is that first wave covers all existing residential units in the two main city clusters, excluding any commercial or mixed-use floors.

@housing manager, can you use T1 to map current processes for three representative buildings in those clusters and highlight what changes when we centralise, feeding into A1? I will take the lead on T2 to shape the operating model and RACI.

Before we lock this in, I would like confirmation from all of you that this scope is workable for the first 30 days.

Thanks for framing this. From an operations side, focusing on the two main city clusters makes sense and keeps travel and coordination manageable.

For T1, I suggest we pick: one newer building with lifts and underground parking, one older walk-up, and one mixed-size block with more frequent tenant changeovers. That will give us a good spread of maintenance, inspections and tenant issues to feed into A1.

One question: do we include any units currently under light refurbishment in this first wave, or do we keep it to fully operational units only?

From the leasing side, I support starting with the two city clusters and excluding commercial. That keeps the rental documentation and marketing messages simpler.

For the operating model in A1 and T2, we should be clear where leasing decisions sit centrally versus on-site. For example, who approves rent discounts or incentives, and who signs off on exceptions to standard rental terms.

On the refurbishment question raised by 48703, my instinct is to include only units that can be let within the next 60 days, so that the new processes actually get tested on live tenancies.

From the buildings side, the two city clusters are fine. It will help if we have one clear way of logging issues and inspections.

On refurb units: some of them are mid-works and not safe for visits yet. I would keep those out of the first wave. We can still add them to the inventory later once they are ready.

For T1, I can support by sharing current inspection routines and ad-hoc maintenance patterns for the buildings we pick.

I can help coordinate inputs for A1 and T2. Just to check I understood: first wave is only existing residential units in the two main city clusters, and we leave out commercial and refurb units for now.

If that is correct, I will start a simple overview list so we all see which buildings are in scope and who the main contact is for each.

Yes, that matches my understanding. For the overview list, please also add current occupancy and any known major technical constraints per building. That will help when we later design the maintenance and inspection schedule and link it to A1.

On the refurb question: I agree with the comments so far. Let us keep the first wave to fully operational units and those that can realistically be let in the next couple of months. Refurb-only units can follow once we have tested the model.

I will reflect that in the draft of A1 and in the scope section of T2.

On T1, I can have first process maps ready for three buildings by mid-week. I will map: tenant onboarding and changeover, maintenance request handling, inspections, rent collection touchpoints, and complaint handling.

I will also flag where we currently rely on individual staff knowledge rather than documented steps. Those are the areas where centralisation and A1 can bring the most benefit.

When you map tenant onboarding and changeover in T1, could you also note which documents are used today and where they differ by building or by staff member? That will help me later when I work on the rental agreement pack and align it with the centralised model in A1.

Good point. I will capture the current rental forms, addenda and any building-specific clauses as part of T1. I will tag where they are driven by regulation versus habit, so we can clean that up when A1 and the new contract pack are defined.

For the process maps in T1, do you have a preferred format? I can set up a simple flowchart template and a place in the shared drive so we all use the same structure and can later link it directly into A1.

A simple swimlane flow per process would work well, with lanes for central office, on-site staff, and external parties. If you can set that up and share a link, I will use it for T1 so that it feeds cleanly into A1 and later into T2.

On T2, my plan is to draft the centralised operating model around four core streams: leasing, maintenance, billing, and complaints. For each, we will define who does what centrally versus on-site, and escalation paths.

Once I have a first draft of A1 and the RACI from T2, I will share here for review by 48703 and 52814 before we take it to senior management.

For the maintenance stream in A1 and T2, please make sure we keep a simple way for on-site staff to log issues, ideally something that works on a phone. If reporting becomes too heavy, it will be hard to keep up in busy periods.

Agree. In the operating model A1, I will propose that we standardise a short digital form for issue logging with a few mandatory fields only. That should keep it usable for on-site staff while still giving us enough data for planning.

To summarise where we are on scope before we move on:

- First rollout wave: all existing residential units in the two main city clusters.
- Excluded: commercial units and units under full refurbishment that are not lettable in the next couple of months.

Unless there are strong objections today, I suggest we treat this as our agreed scope for the first wave and proceed with T1 and T2 on that basis.
No objections from me. The defined scope is clear and workable from a leasing and contract perspective. I will align my later work on the rental templates with this first-wave definition.
Aligned from operations as well. I will proceed with T1 using the agreed scope and will highlight any surprises that might require us to adjust A1 later.

Given the confirmations, we will lock in that scope for the first wave.

Next, I will circulate a draft of A1 based on early inputs from T1 and my work on T2. Once you have reviewed it, we can formally approve the centralised operating model for use in the pilot buildings.

I have now reviewed the latest draft of A1 and the RACI from T2. From an operational and regulatory standpoint, the model is workable for the first wave, provided we keep the feedback loop open during the pilot.

I recommend we approve this version of A1 as the baseline centralised operating model for the rollout, with any changes tracked as we learn from the pilot.

I have also gone through A1. The split of responsibilities between central leasing and on-site staff is clear enough for us to start aligning the rental documentation and communication. I support approving this version for the pilot, with the understanding that we may refine some details after we see it in action.

Thanks for the reviews. Based on your feedback, we will treat the current A1 and the RACI from T2 as the approved centralised operating model for the first rollout wave and the pilot.

Any adjustments we identify during implementation will be logged and incorporated into a later version, but this is now our reference for roles and processes.

threads.thread_goal: Define and finalise tenant lifecycle documents and checklists.

messages.text:
I have put together a first draft of the tenant onboarding and changeover checklist for T3, which will become A2.

The structure is:
- Pre-move-in: application, screening, contract signing, deposit, initial communication.
- Move-in day: keys, meter readings, property condition photos, handover form.
- During tenancy: contact channels, maintenance requests, rent payment reminders.
- Move-out: notice handling, inspection, meter readings, keys return, final photos.

This is based on current practices plus some standardisation ideas. Please review and let me know what is missing or too detailed, so we can finalise A2 and align it with the rental templates in A3, T4 and the FAQ work in T9.

Thanks for sharing. Overall structure of A2 looks good and matches the lifecycle we mapped in T1.

A few suggestions:
- Pre-move-in: add a step to verify compliance documents for the unit (safety certificates, energy performance) before we confirm the move-in date.
- Move-in day: make property condition photos mandatory, with a minimum set of rooms and key technical elements.
- Move-out: include a check for any outstanding maintenance tickets so we do not close the file while something is still open.

These will help us stay aligned with regulations and reduce disputes later.

From the contract side, we should make sure A2 lines up with A3 and T4 so that staff know exactly when each document is used.

I suggest we:
- Link each step in A2 to the specific contract or addendum from A3.
- Add a check that the tenant has received the tenant-facing FAQ from T9 before move-in.
- Clarify who signs off on any non-standard clauses, so we do not have ad-hoc agreements.

I can draft the updated rental agreement templates in A3 this week and share them here for review.

On the practical side, for move-in and move-out in A2, it would help if the checklist is short enough to use on a phone while walking through the unit.

Could we group some of the smaller items under a few clear headings, like safety, cleanliness, and utilities? That way on-site staff can move through the unit logically without missing key points.

Thanks for the detailed comments. I will add the compliance verification step before move-in, make photos mandatory with a defined list, and include the check for open maintenance tickets at move-out.

I will also try to keep the layout of A2 simple so it works on a phone, as 167424 mentioned.

Good point on usability. We can define a core set of mandatory items in A2 and keep optional notes separate. That should keep the checklist short while still covering safety and condition.

Also, for inspections during tenancy, we should align A2 with the maintenance and inspection schedule that will sit in A5, so tenants get consistent messages about when we visit.

Quick update on T4: I have started drafting A3 with a standard rental agreement plus addenda for things like pets, parking, and furnished units.

I will make sure each document is clearly referenced in A2 so staff know which form to use at which step. Once I have a full draft, I will send it to legal for review before we consider it final.

Looking at this from a risk and reputation angle, I want to be sure that A2 and A3 together give tenants a clear and consistent experience.

Two asks:
- Make sure the checklist in A2 explicitly mentions how tenants can raise complaints and how we respond.
- Ensure that the FAQ from T9 is referenced both in A2 and in the contract pack A3, so tenants know where to find practical information.

Once legal has reviewed A3, I would like a short summary of key changes before I sign off.

Understood. I will add a clear step in A2 where we explain complaint channels and expected response times, and I will reference the FAQ from T9 there.

Once 128593 has the updated A3 back from legal, I can help summarise the main changes for you.

When A3 is ready, please flag any clauses that might affect how we handle inspections or maintenance access, so we can make sure A2 and the maintenance schedule in A5 do not conflict with notice periods or tenant rights.

Good call. I will highlight those clauses in A3 and cross-check them against the inspection and access steps in A2. If there is any doubt, I will ask legal to confirm that our notice templates in T9 are aligned.

For the mid-tenancy inspections in A2, it would help if we can group them with the compliance checklist from T12 where possible, so we do not disturb tenants more than needed. Maybe we can note in A2 that some visits will cover both condition and safety checks.

I will add a note in A2 that some inspections combine general condition and safety checks, and that tenants will be informed of the purpose in the notice templates from T9. That should make visits more predictable for them.

Update on T4: legal has now reviewed A3. They confirmed alignment with current rental regulations and added a few clarifications on notice periods and access rights.

From my side, A3 is ready to be used in the pilot, provided we keep an eye on any recurring negotiation points that might require future tweaks.

I have reviewed the latest version of A2 after the updates. It now covers documentation, keys, meter readings, property condition photos, complaint channels, and links to the FAQ from T9.

From an operational standpoint, it is complete enough for us to use in the pilot, and it is still short enough for on-site staff to follow.
I tested the checklist in A2 on a recent move-out. It was manageable on a phone and helped me remember photos and meter readings. I support using this version in the pilot buildings.

Based on your feedback and the test run, I propose we approve the current A2 as the standard tenant onboarding and changeover checklist for the pilot.

If there are no objections by tomorrow, we will treat this version as final for the first rollout wave.

Given legal sign-off on A3 and the alignment with A2 and T9, I recommend we approve A3 for use in the pilot buildings. Any unusual owner or tenant requests that fall outside these templates can be escalated for case-by-case review.

Agreed. With legal confirmation and your recommendation, we will approve A3 as the standard rental agreement and contract pack for the pilot.

Together with the approved A2 checklist, this gives us a consistent tenant lifecycle for the first wave.

threads.thread_goal: Plan maintenance, inspections and compliance activities.

messages.text:
I have drafted an initial proposal for the maintenance and inspection schedule for T6, which will feed into the Maintenance and Inspection Master Schedule A5.

Proposal by building category:
- Newer buildings (under 15 years): annual full inspection, quarterly common-area checks, and statutory safety checks as required.
- Older buildings (15 years and above): full inspection every 6 months, quarterly common-area checks, and more frequent checks on known risk areas.
- Small blocks: annual inspection plus visits triggered by tenant reports.

This is based on the current inventory and condition data we have in A4 and my experience with building codes. Please review and suggest adjustments, especially around combining these with the compliance checklist from T12 so we minimise tenant disruption.

From what I see on site, the proposed frequencies are reasonable, especially the more frequent checks for older buildings.

To make this workable, we should:
- Group inspections by area so we can cover several nearby buildings in one round.
- Combine general condition checks with the safety and energy items from T12 where possible.

I can help refine A5 once we have the full inventory from T5 updated in A4.

From a tenant and owner communication angle, it is important that the inspection frequencies in A5 match what we say in the rental agreements A3 and the notices from T9.

If we go with 6-monthly inspections for older buildings, we should make that clear in the contract and FAQ so tenants are not surprised by visits.

I can help by setting up A5 as a shared sheet with filters by building type, age, and location. That should make it easier for 167424 and other caretakers to plan routes.

Just to confirm: for the compliance checklist in T12, do we want all items to be mandatory for every building, or will there be exceptions by building type?

For T12, my view is that the core health, safety and energy items should be mandatory for all buildings, regardless of age. Some additional checks might be specific to certain systems, but the baseline should be the same.

We can mark optional items in T12, but the main checklist should apply portfolio-wide.
Agree on having one baseline checklist in T12. It makes training easier. We can add a short note for items that only apply if the building has certain systems, like lifts or underground parking.

On grouping by area, once T5 is complete and A4 is up to date, we can cluster buildings by postcode and building type in A5. That will help us plan inspection routes and reduce travel time.

We should also flag in A5 any buildings with known high-risk issues so they get priority slots.

Looking at this from a risk perspective, I want to be sure that our inspection frequencies in A5 are clearly in line with safety and energy regulations.

Can we double-check the proposed intervals against regulatory guidance, especially for fire safety and gas installations, before we finalise A5? If needed, we can ask the legal and compliance team to confirm.

Yes, I will cross-check the proposed frequencies with current regulations and manufacturer recommendations. For any grey areas, I will ask legal and compliance to validate before we lock A5.

In practice, our proposal is already slightly more frequent than the minimum in most cases, which should give us a safety margin.
Once A4 is fully updated from T5, I can propose a first pass of grouped inspection routes in A5 for the two main city clusters. That will show if the schedule is realistic in terms of workload.

I have created the initial structure for A5 with columns for building ID, type, age band, location, inspection type, frequency, and next due date. Once T5 and T12 are final, we can populate and standardise the entries.

I have now incorporated feedback and regulatory checks into the proposal for A5:
- Newer buildings: annual full inspection plus statutory checks.
- Older buildings: full inspection every 6 months plus statutory checks.
- Small blocks: annual inspection plus triggered visits.

All of these include the mandatory items from T12. I propose we adopt this as our standard inspection frequency and scope for each building category.

From my side, these frequencies are acceptable and can be reflected in the tenant communication and contract wording. As long as we keep tenants informed via the notices from T9, this should not create undue friction.
The updated schedule in A5 looks workable. The 6-monthly checks for older buildings will help us catch issues earlier. I support using this as the standard going forward.
Given the confirmations and the regulatory check you mentioned, I am comfortable approving these inspection frequencies and scopes in A5 as our standard for the first wave.

On T12, I have reviewed the checklist items and aligned them with regulatory requirements: fire safety, access, ventilation, and energy performance are all included as mandatory items.

I propose we confirm T12 as the standard compliance checklist for all buildings, with only a few conditional items marked as 'if applicable'.
I have tested T12 on one of the older buildings. It covers the key safety and energy points without being too long. I support using it as the standard checklist for all buildings.

With your test and the regulatory alignment, we will confirm T12 as the mandatory compliance checklist across the portfolio. Any future regulatory changes can be handled as updates to this single list.

threads.thread_goal: Agree on KPIs, dashboard structure and reporting cadence.

messages.text:
I have created a first version of the property performance dashboard template for T7, which is now set up as A6.

Current KPIs:
- Occupancy rate by building and overall.
- Rent arrears (amount and percentage).
- Number of open maintenance issues and average age.
- Inspection status from A5 (on track, overdue).
- Number of complaints and average resolution time.

Please review and suggest any additional metrics or simplifications. We also need to agree how often we share this with owners and senior management, and who updates which fields, as per T7 and T8.

The initial set of KPIs in A6 covers the essentials. I would add:
- Turnaround time between move-out and next move-in, to track how quickly we re-let units.
- Percentage of inspections completed on time, linked to A5.

We should also keep the number of metrics manageable so on-site staff are not overwhelmed with data entry.

From a leasing and owner perspective, occupancy, arrears, and turnaround time are key. I would also consider:
- Average achieved rent versus target, to see if we are pricing correctly.

We should avoid too many detailed financial metrics in A6, though, and leave deeper analysis to finance.

For on-site staff, it would help if A6 clearly shows which data we need to update and how often. For example, inspections and open issues could be updated weekly, while some financial data might be monthly.

For senior management, I would like A6 to give a quick view of:
- Occupancy.
- Arrears.
- Major issues or risks.

We can keep the dashboard simple and use it in a monthly review. For owners, a quarterly summary might be enough, unless there are specific issues.

I will add turnaround time and on-time inspection percentage to A6, and mark them as core KPIs.

For data entry, I will highlight which fields are updated by housing management, on-site staff, and finance, in line with T7.

On cadence, I suggest:
- Internal team: weekly review of A6 to catch issues early.
- Senior management: monthly summary based on A6.
- Owners: quarterly report, with ad-hoc updates if there are major incidents.

This should balance transparency with workload.
I support that cadence. For owners, the quarterly report can highlight occupancy, arrears, and any significant maintenance or compliance actions, without going into too much operational detail.

If we go with a weekly internal review, I can commit to updating inspection status and open issues in A6 once a week for my buildings. It would help if the dashboard clearly flags overdue items so we can prioritise.
I will add simple colour coding in A6 for overdue inspections and long-open issues, so they stand out in the weekly review.

Looking at the updated A6, I think the final set of KPIs should be:
- Occupancy rate.
- Rent arrears.
- Turnaround time between tenancies.
- Open maintenance issues and average age.
- Inspection completion rate.
- Complaints volume and resolution time.

Additional metrics like achieved rent versus target can be optional for now. This keeps the dashboard focused and actionable.
I am comfortable with that list as the core KPIs in A6. We can always add more detail later if needed, but this covers the main drivers of performance.
Agreed. Let us lock these as the standard KPIs for A6. They give a clear picture without being overwhelming.

On reporting cadence, I support the proposal:
- Weekly internal review using A6.
- Monthly summary for senior management.
- Quarterly report for owners, with ad-hoc updates for major issues.

We can formalise this in the communication plan under T8.
That cadence works for operations. We will build the weekly review into our routine and use it to catch issues before they show up in the monthly and quarterly reports.
I will update T7 and T8 to reflect the agreed KPIs and reporting cadence, and I will document who updates which parts of A6 and when.

threads.thread_goal: Prepare pilot rollout, communication and incident handling approach.

messages.text:
For the pilot of the centralised model under T10, I propose we use two buildings:
- Building Alpha: newer, high-occupancy block in the first city cluster.
- Building Beta: older walk-up with more frequent tenant changeovers in the second cluster.

Both are fully residential and already well documented in the inventory A4. They give us a good mix of stability and complexity.

I have also drafted a simple communication outline for owners and tenants, based on A7, to explain what the pilot means for them. Please review the building choices and the communication approach before we confirm the pilot start date.

From an on-site perspective, Alpha and Beta are good choices. I know both buildings well and can support the pilot activities there.

We should make sure the maintenance and inspection schedule from A5 is fully set up for these two before we start, so we do not confuse tenants with changing dates mid-pilot.

From the leasing side, Alpha and Beta will give us a good test of the new A2 checklist and A3 contract pack. Alpha has more stable tenants, while Beta will likely see more move-ins and move-outs during the pilot.

For owners, we should clearly explain in the A7 communication pack what changes for them in terms of reporting and decision-making, and what stays the same.

I can help refine the owner and tenant messages in A7 and align them with the FAQ and notices from T9.

Do we have a target start date in mind for the pilot in Alpha and Beta, or should we first confirm that all required documents and checklists (A2, A3, A5, A8) are ready?

Alpha and Beta sound like sensible pilot choices. Before we confirm, I want to be sure that:
- Owners of both buildings are comfortable with the pilot and the centralised model.
- We have a clear incident and escalation procedure in place via A8 and T11.

Once those are in place, I would like us to set a firm pilot start date within the next two weeks.

On T11, I have drafted an incident and escalation procedure that will become A8. It defines incident categories, severity levels, and response time targets, and sets out who is contacted at each step.

I will share it with 48703 and 167424 for practical feedback before we finalise it for the pilot.

I have reviewed the draft A8. The categories and response times look reasonable. It would help if we include a simple step-by-step guide for on-site staff, so in an urgent situation they do not have to read a long document.

I agree. A8 covers the right escalation paths. For the pilot, we should also make sure contact details are up to date and that there is a clear backup if someone is unavailable.

Once we add a short quick-reference section, I am comfortable using A8 in Alpha and Beta.
I will add a one-page quick guide to A8 with clear steps for each severity level, plus contact numbers. Then I will share the updated version for final confirmation.

For A7, I have drafted:
- An owner briefing explaining the benefits of the centralised model, service levels, and reporting cadence from T8.
- A tenant notice explaining what changes in day-to-day contact, inspections, and maintenance requests.

I will align the language with the FAQ and notices from T9 so tenants get consistent messages.

On timing, if we can finalise A7 and A8 this week and confirm owner consent for Alpha and Beta, we could start the pilot on the first of next month. That gives us enough time to brief on-site staff and update A4 and A5 for these buildings.

The first of next month works for me as a target pilot start date, assuming we have owner agreement and the communication pack ready.

I will reach out to the owners of Alpha and Beta to explain the pilot and get their confirmation, using the owner briefing from A7 as a base.
Once the start date is confirmed, I will schedule the first round of inspections and any planned maintenance in A5 for Alpha and Beta, and make sure tenants receive the notices from T9 in time.

The updated A8 with the quick guide is now ready. It defines incident categories, severity levels, escalation paths, and response time targets, and has been reviewed by 48703 and 167424.

I recommend we approve A8 for use in the pilot, so everyone knows how to handle incidents in Alpha and Beta.

I have reviewed the owner and tenant messages in A7. They clearly explain the centralised model, service levels, and how often owners and tenants will hear from us, in line with T8 and the dashboard cadence.

From an operational side, I support using this pack for the pilot.

I have now spoken with the owners of Alpha and Beta. They are comfortable with the pilot and the centralised model, provided they receive the quarterly reports and can escalate issues via the channels in A8.

Given that, I propose we confirm Alpha and Beta as the pilot buildings and set the pilot start date for the first of next month.
Confirmed from operations: Alpha and Beta are ready for the pilot, and the first of next month is realistic for the start date. We will use that date to align all preparatory work under T10.

With your confirmation on A7 and the earlier feedback on A8, I am comfortable approving both the owner and tenant communication pack A7 and the incident procedure A8 for use in the pilot.

These, together with the selected pilot buildings and start date, give us a clear framework for the rollout.

Great. I will brief the leasing team on the pilot specifics for Alpha and Beta, including the use of A2, A3, A7, and A8, so they know exactly how to handle new tenancies and incidents during the pilot.
I will brief on-site staff in Alpha and Beta on the new checklists and procedures, and make sure they know where to find A7 and A8 and who to call for escalations.
